cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: Sitting en banc the court overruled In re K.M.T. and held that an order changing a neglected child's permanency goal from reunification to adoption is an immediately appealable final order, that permanency goal review hearings must protect parental due process, that the court must first find by a preponderance that the government made reasonable efforts toward reunification, and that a finding of parental unfitness must precede termination absent truly exceptional circumstances or stipulation.
cases.quote: a change of the presumptive goal of a neglect proceeding from reunification to adoption is an appealable final order

relevance.ACT-02: It conditions any court-ordered service plan and goal change on a preponderance finding that the government made reasonable efforts consistent with the neglect plan.
relevance.ACT-04: It requires the trial court to give weighty consideration to the parents' preferred relative caregiver before approving a competing stranger adoption.
relevance.OUT-01: It makes the abandonment of reunification a discrete, appealable decision that the government must justify with proof of reasonable efforts.
relevance.OUT-02: It holds that parental unfitness must be found before parental rights are terminated through TPR or contested adoption absent truly exceptional circumstances.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the D.C. decision that created appellate review of the goal-change decision that previously escaped correction entirely.
relevance.FAIL-03: It ties the District's compliance with the federal reasonable-efforts requirement to a judicially enforceable finding at the permanency hearing.
relevance.PMC-01: Its reasonable-efforts finding requirement is the courtroom analogue of the CFSR permanency measures PMC tracks.
relevance.PMC-06: It is the single most important structural holding a cross-jurisdiction analysis of D.C. permanency decision-making must account for.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: An unwed father was constitutionally entitled to a hearing on his fitness before his children were taken from him, and Illinois' presumption that unwed fathers are unfit denied him due process and equal protection.
cases.quote: as a matter of due process of law, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him

relevance.INP-05: It establishes that a parent who comes forward seeking his children may not be treated as presumptively unfit by category.
relevance.INP-12: It is the baseline rule that removal of children from a parent requires an individualized hearing on fitness, not a categorical presumption.
relevance.DEC-04: It condemns removal decisions made by presumption rather than by individualized proof about this parent.
relevance.FAIL-05: It is the Supreme Court's holding that classifying parents by status rather than conduct violates equal protection.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: As applied, Washington's broad third-party visitation statute violated the mother's due process rights because the trial court gave no special weight to the presumption that a fit parent acts in her children's best interests.
cases.quote: there is a presumption that fit parents act in the best interests of their children

relevance.INP-05: It protects the decisions of a parent who seeks help voluntarily from being second-guessed absent a finding of unfitness.
relevance.DEC-06: It supports resolving cases through voluntary, non-court service pathways where the parent is fit and no petition is warranted.
relevance.ACT-01: It is the constitutional reason a voluntary service plan must rest on parental agreement rather than state substitution of judgment.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a State to protect a child from private violence, so caseworkers who left Joshua in his abusive father's custody were not liable under § 1983; a duty arises only where the State takes the person into its own custody.
cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

relevance.OUT-06: It is the reason a § 1983 claim for a child killed in the parental home usually fails, pushing families toward D.C. tort law instead.
relevance.FAIL-04: It draws the custody line that determines whether a death under agency supervision is a constitutional violation or only a tort.
relevance.FAIL-02: Its custody rationale is the flip side of unlawful removal: state action, not inaction, is what the Due Process Clause reaches.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Domicile under ICWA is a matter of uniform federal law; because the twins took their mother's reservation domicile at birth the tribal court had exclusive jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(a) and the state adoption decree had to be vacated.
cases.quote: the twin babies in this case were domiciled on the reservation when adoption proceedings were begun, the Choctaw tribal court possessed exclusive jurisdiction

relevance.INP-11: It is the controlling authority on when an Indian child's case must go to tribal rather than District court at the threshold.
relevance.ACT-04: It shows that tribal jurisdiction and ICWA placement policy can displace an otherwise valid local placement or adoption.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court rejected every challenge to the Indian Child Welfare Act, upholding Congress's Article I power and rejecting the anticommandeering claims on the merits while dismissing the equal protection and nondelegation claims for lack of standing.
cases.quote: we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute

relevance.INP-11: It confirms that ICWA's active-efforts, expert-witness and placement-preference commands remain binding on courts handling Indian child custody proceedings.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit
cases.holding: Individual District caseworkers had qualified immunity on the Fourth and Fifth Amendment claims because the contours of the exigency exception for warrantless child removals were not clearly established, but summary judgment for the District itself was vacated and remanded for Monell analysis of the removal policies.
cases.quote: the precise contours of when an exigency exists to justify removal without a warrant or pre-deprivation hearing are not settled

relevance.INP-12: It is the D.C. Circuit's statement of the constitutional test governing protective custody taken without a court order.
relevance.DEC-04: It holds that in an exigency the District may seize children without a court order, but leaves the standard for exigency unsettled in this circuit.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the controlling circuit authority on § 1983 wrongful-removal claims in the District, including qualified immunity and municipal liability.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit
cases.holding: A youth in the District's legal custody and placed by it in a group program was in state custody for DeShaney purposes, so the District owed him a substantive due process duty of care and the jury's deliberate-indifference verdict was sustained.
cases.quote: Because the District, rather than Tron's family, had primary legal control over him, the District had legal responsibility for his daily care.

relevance.ACT-03: It establishes that once the District places a child it assumes a constitutional duty to select and monitor the placement with care.
relevance.OUT-04: It applied the custody duty to an older youth in a District placement program, which matters for youth remaining in care past eighteen.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the circuit authority under which a death or serious injury in a District placement can be a constitutional violation.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the leading D.C. Circuit case imposing § 1983 liability on the District for deliberate indifference in selecting and monitoring a placement provider.
relevance.PMC-04: It shows what a fatality review's findings about placement selection and monitoring can support in litigation.

cases.court: United States District Court for the District of Columbia
cases.holding: After trial the court found the District's child welfare system violated federal and District statutory and constitutional requirements at nearly every stage, including a consistent failure to provide services or make reasonable efforts to prevent placement, and ordered systemic relief.
cases.quote: the Court finds that defendants have consistently failed to provide services or otherwise use “reasonable efforts” to prevent placement

relevance.INP-09: It is the D.C. class action in which court-supervised oversight of the entire child welfare system originated.
relevance.DEC-06: Its findings about the absence of preventive services are the factual baseline against which any District differential-response claim must be measured.
relevance.ACT-01: It found that voluntary and preventive services were largely unavailable in the District, so 'voluntary services' often existed only on paper.
relevance.ACT-02: It found chronic failures in case planning and in the timely preparation of plans required by federal and District law.
relevance.ACT-03: It found that children were consistently not placed in the least restrictive placement consistent with their needs.
relevance.OUT-04: It documented foster care drift that leaves youth in care to age out without permanency.
relevance.FAIL-03: It is the judicial finding that the District failed the federal Title IV-E and IV-B requirements that fund its system.
relevance.PMC-01: It is the litigation record against which CFSR performance in the District should be read.
relevance.PMC-02: Its findings on service capacity and record-keeping are the template for auditing where District child welfare money does and does not go.
relevance.PMC-03: It illustrates why independent external review of District CPS policy has been necessary.
relevance.PMC-06: It is the foundational systemic-failure dataset for any cross-layer analysis of the District's chain.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: A plaintiff suing the District for negligent placement and monitoring of a foster child who died must present expert testimony on the applicable standard of care, and the foster mother was not the District's agent for respondeat superior purposes.
cases.quote: Mrs. Hampton should have presented expert testimony on the standard of care, and that the absence of such testimony was fatal to her case

relevance.INP-01: It defines what a plaintiff must prove about social work practice when a report was made and the agency's later handling is challenged.
relevance.INP-09: It shows that establishing a deviation from child-welfare practice standards requires expert proof, not just an audit finding.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the leading D.C. case on what a family must prove to recover for a child's death while under agency supervision.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the practical barrier, expert testimony on the standard of care, that defeats most D.C. claims arising from a death in foster care.
relevance.PMC-04: It explains why fatality review findings alone do not establish negligence without expert standard-of-care proof.

cases.case_name: Doe ex rel. Fein v. District of Columbia
cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: Police reports of a child's injuries did not satisfy the six-month written notice requirement of D.C. Code § 12-309, and the statute does not permit equitable tolling, so the abused child's claims against the District and its employees were barred.
cases.quote: the police reports filed after Jane Doe suffered her physical injuries were insufficient under D.C.Code § 12-309 to provide the District with notice of her potential claims

relevance.INP-02: It shows that a report to authorities does not by itself preserve the reported child's later claim against the District.
relevance.DEC-01: It arose from an allegation that DHS failed to investigate and failed to check on other children in the home, the classic screen-out failure.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the notice trap that most often extinguishes claims arising from serious injury to a child known to the District.
relevance.FAIL-04: It holds that § 12-309's six-month notice period is jurisdictional in effect and cannot be equitably tolled, even for an injured infant.
relevance.PMC-04: It demonstrates why delayed fatality or serious-injury review can leave a family with no remedy at all.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: When CPS receives a report identifying particular children as abused, the Child Abuse Prevention Act creates a special relationship imposing on the District a duty to take the steps the Act prescribes for those children, so summary judgment for the District was error.
cases.quote: From that moment on, the District had a duty to take certain steps prescribed by the Act for the protection of those children.

relevance.INP-01: It is the D.C. case holding that a mandated report to CPS about identified children triggers a legally enforceable duty to act.
relevance.INP-02: It applies equally to any report that specifically and individually identifies the children at risk.
relevance.INP-06: It makes a hotline report the trigger that converts the District's general public duty into a special duty to the named children.
relevance.INP-08: A school or other reporter's identification of specific children is what starts the District's statutory duty running.
relevance.INP-10: It measures the District's liability by whether CPS took the affirmative investigative steps the Act required after intake.
relevance.DEC-01: It holds that failure to take the Act's prescribed steps after a report can defeat summary judgment for the District.
relevance.DEC-02: It defines the investigative conduct the Child Abuse Prevention Act required once a report was accepted.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the doctrinal gateway for a damages claim when reported children are later seriously harmed.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the leading D.C. special-relationship case for holding the District liable after harm to children it was told about.
relevance.PMC-03: It shows that the statutory duties a citizen review panel evaluates are judicially enforceable obligations, not aspirations.

cases.case_name: V.K. v. Child & Family Services Agency
cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: On judicial review of a CFSA administrative decision upholding a 'substantiated' abuse entry in the Child Protection Register, CFSA bears the burden by a preponderance at the fair hearing and the court will disturb the hearing officer's finding only if the record compels a contrary conclusion; the decision was affirmed on substantial evidence.
cases.quote: At the hearing, CFSA bore the burden of proof by a preponderance of the evidence.

relevance.INP-01: It is the case that shows how a report by a professional becomes a substantiated Register entry naming the reported adult.
relevance.INP-08: The substantiation there rested partly on hearsay from a teacher's report, illustrating how school disclosures drive the finding.
relevance.INP-10: It maps the path from intake through investigation to a recorded substantiation subject to administrative review.
relevance.DEC-02: It describes the evidentiary record, including hearsay, on which CFSA investigations are sustained.
relevance.DEC-03: It is the controlling D.C. authority on the burden of proof and the scope of review for a substantiated finding and Register listing.
relevance.FAIL-06: It sets out the confidentiality and expungement rules governing the Child Protection Register.
relevance.PMC-05: It shows that Register information is confidential by statute and not subject to ordinary public disclosure.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: The trial court properly exercised parens patriae jurisdiction over an adjudicated neglected child to authorize a do-not-resuscitate order, applied the best-interests rather than the substituted-judgment standard where the parents disagreed, and must make that finding by clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: we hold that the standard of proof required for the issuance of a DNR in the best interests of a child is clear and convincing evidence

relevance.INP-04: It is the D.C. case on the court's own authority to act for a neglected child when a medical decision must be made.
relevance.INP-07: It arose from the medical setting and governs how healthcare decisions for a child in care reach the court.
relevance.ACT-05: It shows the court's protective authority over a committed child extends to overriding a parent's objection.
relevance.ACT-06: It supplies the standard, clear and convincing evidence of best interests, for court-authorized emergency medical decisions for a child in care.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: Before terminating the commitment of a neglected child prior to the child's twenty-first birthday the court must find that commitment is no longer necessary to safeguard the child's welfare, and it must consider the child's best interest; the court's neglect obligations continue after the child turns eighteen.
cases.quote: we hold that the best interest of the child must be considered when the court acts to terminate the commitment of a child

relevance.INP-05: It confirms that a youth who is still a minor for neglect purposes may invoke the court's continuing duty to provide for care.
relevance.OUT-04: It is the controlling D.C. authority that neglect jurisdiction and the duty to provide care run to the twenty-first birthday, not eighteen.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: Civil Rule 36 admissions deemed against parents who failed to respond were conclusively established and, with the rest of the evidence, sufficed to prove neglect by a preponderance, so the adjudication was affirmed.
cases.quote: The government’s burden at trial was to prove that K.M. was neglected by a preponderance of the evidence.

relevance.INP-10: It shows how the investigative allegations carry forward into the formal adjudication once a case is escalated.
relevance.DEC-03: It states the evidentiary standard the government must meet to establish that a child is neglected.
relevance.DEC-05: It is the current D.C. statement of the burden of proof at the neglect factfinding hearing after a petition is filed.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: The Improved Child Abuse Investigations Amendment Act of 2002 does not bar Superior Court judges from admitting the results of court-ordered mental evaluations in neglect hearings, such examinations under D.C. Code § 16-2315(e)(4) are not shielded by the doctor-patient privilege, and the neglect adjudication was supported by sufficient evidence.
cases.quote: we hold that the trial court's neglect adjudication was supported by sufficient evidence

relevance.INP-04: It governs court-ordered mental examinations of a parent that the judge directs during a neglect case.
relevance.DEC-02: It resolves what evaluation evidence gathered during the assessment phase may be used against a parent.
relevance.DEC-05: It addresses the admissibility and privilege questions that recur at the neglect factfinding hearing.
relevance.OUT-05: It marks the evidentiary line between an adjudication that will be sustained and one that must be vacated for insufficiency.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: A parent who does not timely move for review of a magistrate judge's neglect and disposition order by a Superior Court associate judge forfeits appellate review, and the Court of Appeals affirmed the dismissal of the untimely motion without reaching the merits.
cases.quote: We therefore affirm the Superior Court’s order dismissing the motion for review as untimely, and conclude that the merits of the neglect ruling are not properly before us.

relevance.DEC-05: It fixes the procedural step a parent must take after a magistrate judge's neglect ruling to preserve any challenge.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the D.C. rule that failure to seek timely associate-judge review forecloses correction of an erroneous neglect adjudication.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: Reasonable efforts require CFSA to identify the barriers to reunification and to refer the parent to appropriate services addressing them; CFSA satisfied that duty here and the change of permanency goal from reunification to adoption was affirmed.
cases.quote: requires the District to identify the barriers to reunification and prepare a case plan by recommending appropriate services designed to address the needs of each child and family

relevance.DEC-06: It explains that the District's obligation is to make services accessible, which is what a non-court service response must also deliver.
relevance.ACT-01: It holds that a social worker cannot compel treatment but must ensure the parent has access to it.
relevance.ACT-02: It is the leading post-Ta.L. D.C. decision defining the content of a court-ordered case plan and the reasonable efforts that must accompany it.
relevance.OUT-01: It sets out the three-part showing the government must make before abandoning reunification as the goal.
relevance.FAIL-03: It reads the District's reasonable-efforts duty against the federal ASFA framework it implements.
relevance.PMC-01: It is the case-level test corresponding to the CFSR permanency and service-provision measures.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: The ADA and the Rehabilitation Act protect parents with disabilities from discriminatory curtailment of parental rights and require reasonable accommodations, but the trial court did not violate them where the intellectually disabled mother received extensive services and still could not safely parent, so the goal change to adoption was affirmed.
cases.quote: The ADA and the Rehabilitation Act do protect parents with disabilities, including intellectual and psychiatric disabilities, from discriminatory curtailment of their parental rights.

relevance.ACT-02: It requires that the service plan itself be accommodated to a parent's disability rather than set at an unreachable standard.
relevance.OUT-01: It is the D.C. authority on when a disabled parent's failure to progress may lawfully end reunification efforts.
relevance.FAIL-05: It is the only published D.C. appellate decision applying federal disability antidiscrimination law to child welfare decision-making.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: The trial court has power to protect a child from the harmful effects of compelled testimony in a neglect case, but ordinarily must exercise it through conditions on the examination rather than by barring the child's testimony outright; excluding the children's testimony and the parent's expert required a new trial.
cases.quote: We hold that the trial court does have power to protect a child from the harmful effects of forced testimony.

relevance.INP-04: It defines the court's protective authority over how a child is questioned once the case is before it.
relevance.DEC-02: It governs the interviewing and examination of child victims whose statements drove the investigation.
relevance.DEC-05: It is the D.C. rule on child testimony and expert evidence at the neglect factfinding hearing.
relevance.ACT-05: It shows that protective measures for a child must be tailored, not blanket prohibitions.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: Due process does not require clear and convincing evidence for an order of permanent guardianship; the preponderance standard prescribed by D.C. Code § 16-2388(f) is constitutionally sufficient because guardianship does not sever the parent-child relationship.
cases.quote: The principal issue on appeal addresses whether the due process clause of the Constitution requires the more demanding standard of "clear and convincing evidence." We hold that it does not.

relevance.OUT-03: It is the controlling D.C. authority on the burden of proof for permanent guardianship, the kinship permanency alternative to adoption.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: Probable cause supported the medical hold and shelter care of an infant with suspected shaken baby syndrome and the parents' Child Protection Register listing did not violate due process, but the warrantless seizure of the sibling from inside the family home was remanded for a determination whether exigent circumstances existed.
cases.quote: under the Fourth Amendment, a lawful seizure of children from their parents' custody requires a court order, e.g., a warrant, probable cause, or exigent circumstances

relevance.INP-03: It describes the coordinated hospital, police and CFSA response that generated the custody decision.
relevance.INP-07: It holds that a treating specialist's abuse assessment can itself supply probable cause for a medical hold.
relevance.INP-12: It is the leading D.C. decision on the constitutional limits of protective custody taken before any court order.
relevance.DEC-02: It addresses how far CFSA may go during an in-depth investigation before a court order is required.
relevance.DEC-03: It holds that placement on the Child Protection Register following a substantiated finding did not deny the parents due process.
relevance.DEC-04: It states the D.C. rule that emergency removal requires a court order, probable cause or exigency, and applies it to a hospital medical hold.
relevance.ACT-03: It ties the lawfulness of the initial shelter care placement to the same probable cause showing.
relevance.ACT-06: It validates the use of a medical hold to keep an injured infant in hospital care pending investigation.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the D.C. Court of Appeals' framework for a § 1983 claim that children were seized from the home without a warrant or exigency.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: The trial court could not compel the United States Attorney, who was not a party, to produce a recording for the neglect case; a temporary order suspending visitation pending the parent's criminal case was not a final appealable order; and the neglect adjudications were supported by sufficient evidence.
cases.quote: we hold that the visitation order in this case, unlike the order in In re D.M., was not a final order subject to appellate review

relevance.INP-06: The case began with a call to the CFSA child abuse hotline that led directly to the child's removal.
relevance.ACT-05: It is the D.C. authority on the appealability of an order restricting a parent's contact with the child during a neglect case.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: Parents represented by appointed counsel in a termination of parental rights proceeding have a statutory right under D.C. Code § 16-2304(b)(1) to the effective assistance of counsel, and such claims must be raised on direct appeal, by motion filed as early as possible.
cases.quote: we hold that parents who are represented by appointed counsel in a termination of parental rights proceeding have a statutory right to the effective assistance of counsel

relevance.OUT-02: It supplies the D.C. statutory right to effective counsel that goes beyond Lassiter's case-by-case constitutional floor in termination cases.
relevance.FAIL-01: It creates the direct-appeal vehicle by which a termination tainted by deficient appointed counsel can be reversed.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: The trial court permissibly found the repeatedly incarcerated father unfit and waived his consent to the foster parents' adoption, and its brief treatment of the grandmother he proposed sufficed as weighty consideration only because he offered almost no evidence about her.
cases.quote: In most cases, such a brief explanation would be insufficient to demonstrate the trial court’s “weighty consideration” of the parent’s chosen custodian.

relevance.ACT-04: It is the D.C. case on how seriously a court must engage with the relative caregiver a parent proposes before rejecting kinship placement.
relevance.OUT-02: It applies the clear and convincing unfitness standard to an incarcerated parent whose absences left special-needs children without care.
relevance.OUT-03: It shows that an abandoned relative guardianship motion removes that relative as an alternative permanency option.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: The evidence did not show that the mother's back injury and physical incapacity left her children without proper parental care or control, so the neglect adjudication was vacated.
cases.quote: we conclude there is insufficient evidence to support a finding of neglect and vacate the trial court’s holding

relevance.DEC-01: It marks the kind of allegation that should not have survived screening into a substantiated case.
relevance.DEC-03: It shows that parental disability or poverty alone does not supply credible evidence of neglect.
relevance.OUT-05: It is the D.C. example of an adjudication vacated for insufficient evidence, ending the case.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a published reversal of an agency-driven neglect finding for failure of proof.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: D.C. Code § 4-1321.04 confers on good-faith mandatory reporters immunity from liability rather than immunity from suit, so the denial of that immunity is not effectively unreviewable after final judgment and cannot be appealed under the collateral order doctrine; the interlocutory appeal was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
cases.quote: mandatory reporters are shielded from liability, both civil and criminal, for reports made in good faith, even if those reports ultimately turn out to be mistaken

relevance.INP-01: It is the most recent D.C. decision construing the mandatory reporter immunity that accompanies the reporting duty and its criminal penalty for failure to report.
relevance.INP-02: It confirms that immunity attaches to good-faith reports even when the report proves mistaken.
relevance.INP-06: It explains the statutory presumption of good faith that protects hotline reporters from suit for damages.
relevance.INP-07: It arose from a clinician's report and governs the immunity a healthcare reporter can invoke.
relevance.INP-08: It sets the procedural posture in which a school or other reporter must litigate immunity, namely after final judgment rather than by interlocutory appeal.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: Orders barring a father in a neglect proceeding from conferring with his criminal defense counsel about his privilege against self-incrimination, and excluding that lawyer from the courtroom, were immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine and were an abuse of discretion.
cases.quote: the trial court abused its discretion in excluding Mr. Rapping from the courtroom, and in prohibiting T.B. and Mr. Harris from conferring with Mr. Rapping about the neglect proceeding

relevance.DEC-05: It protects a parent's access to counsel of choice once a neglect petition places him at risk of parallel criminal exposure.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a D.C. reversal of trial court orders that interfered with a parent's right to informed legal advice in a neglect case.

cases.case_name: Vining v. Council of the District of Columbia
cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: The Council may not invoke the Legislative Privilege Act through D.C. FOIA Exemption 6 (or, on this record, Exemption 4) to withhold documents responsive to a FOIA request, and summary judgment for the Council was reversed.
cases.quote: We conclude that the Legislative Privilege Act cannot be invoked through Exemption 6 so as to permit the Council to withhold documents responsive to a FOIA request

relevance.INP-09: It keeps legislative oversight records about District agencies reachable by the public rather than sealed by privilege.
relevance.FAIL-06: It is the D.C. decision rejecting a public body's attempt to expand a FOIA exemption to defeat disclosure.
relevance.PMC-02: It preserves public access to the Council records that document agency spending and performance.
relevance.PMC-03: It supports the ability of citizen reviewers to obtain the District records they need to evaluate CPS policy.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the controlling D.C. authority on the narrow construction of D.C. FOIA exemptions.
relevance.PMC-06: It establishes that the District record base a public analysis depends on is presumptively disclosable.

cases.case_name: District of Columbia v. Fraternal Order of Police, Metropolitan Police Department Labor Committee
cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: Under D.C. FOIA's personal privacy exemption the negligible public interest in the identities of employees who sent emails under a pledge of confidentiality did not outweigh their privacy interest, so the District was entitled to withhold the identifying information.
cases.quote: we conclude that FOIA does not require the District of Columbia to disclose the identities of the email authors

relevance.FAIL-06: It defines the personal privacy limit on what a requester can compel a District agency to disclose.
relevance.PMC-02: It governs redaction of individual identities in audit-related District records released under FOIA.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the D.C. authority on the balancing test under the personal privacy exemption to D.C. FOIA.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: The District failed to carry its burden of showing that shelter care was necessary for a healthy five-month-old removed after her mother's hospitalization, even under the less demanding probable cause standard, so the shelter care order was reversed.
cases.quote: Because we conclude that the District failed to carry its burden even under a less-demanding probable-cause standard, we assume without deciding that a probable-cause standard applies.

relevance.INP-03: The case began with a hospital and law enforcement response to a parent's health emergency rather than any allegation of harm to the child.
relevance.INP-12: It is the most recent D.C. decision policing the threshold for keeping a child in emergency protective custody.
relevance.DEC-04: It holds that a parent's untreated mental health issues, without evidence of likely danger to the child, cannot justify emergency removal.
relevance.ACT-03: It reverses the shelter care placement that followed the emergency custody decision.
relevance.ACT-06: It distinguishes a temporary parental medical emergency from a condition warranting state custody of the child.
relevance.OUT-05: It ends the removal by reversal rather than by any finding against the parent.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the leading recent D.C. reversal of an agency emergency custody decision for failure of proof.
relevance.FAIL-02: It shows what an insufficiently supported removal looks like in the District's own appellate court.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: Summarily denying a parent's motion to extend the time to file a late appeal from a neglect finding and disposition, without considering her claim that her lawyer's failure to file constituted excusable neglect, was an abuse of discretion.
cases.quote: it was an abuse of discretion for the trial court summarily to deny the requested extension

relevance.FAIL-01: It is the D.C. authority preserving a parent's late appeal where counsel's default, not the parent's, caused the missed deadline.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the practical route by which a parent whose children were removed can still obtain appellate review after a missed deadline.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: Before terminating parental rights or granting a contested adoption the trial court must expressly determine whether the evidence shows parental unfitness or exceptional circumstances making continuation of the relationship detrimental to the child; because the magistrate judge never articulated that determination the case was remanded.
cases.quote: a natural parent’s unfitness may be evidenced by a variety of behaviors, conditions, and circumstances, including but not limited to past or ongoing child abuse, neglect, maltreatment, or abandonment

relevance.OUT-01: It recognizes that termination may be inappropriate where a parent's unfitness at the time of trial is reasonably likely to be temporary.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the D.C. decision cataloguing what may establish parental unfitness and requiring the trial court to state that finding expressly.

cases.case_name: In re Petition for Adoption of J.S.R.
cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: Adopting a standard higher than the statute required, the court held that a parent's consent to adoption may be waived only on proof by clear and convincing evidence that consent is being withheld contrary to the child's best interests.
cases.quote: We, therefore, hold that parental consent must be shown to have been withheld contrary to the child’s best interests by “clear and convincing” evidence.

relevance.OUT-02: It is the foundational D.C. case establishing the clear and convincing standard for waiving parental consent to adoption.
relevance.OUT-03: It fixes the proof burden that any competing permanency petitioner must satisfy over a parent's objection.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: In competing adoption petitions the parent's choice of a fit custodian, here a maternal great-aunt, must be given weighty consideration that can be overcome only by clear and convincing evidence that the arrangement is clearly contrary to the child's best interest.
cases.quote: a parent's choice of a fit custodian for the child must be given weighty consideration

relevance.INP-05: It protects a parent's own plan for who should care for the child when the parent asks for help rather than being found unfit.
relevance.ACT-04: It is the origin of the D.C. weighty consideration doctrine that favors the relative caregiver a parent selects.
relevance.OUT-03: It governs how a court chooses between a relative and a foster placement for permanency.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: Only the child, not the parent, may take an interlocutory appeal from a shelter care order under D.C. Code § 16-2328(a), and that limitation does not violate due process because the custody deprivation is temporary and followed by a factfinding hearing at which the government must prove its allegations by a preponderance.
cases.quote: Because it is not the child who has brought this appeal (but rather her mother), we lack jurisdiction to entertain it under the plain language of the statute.

relevance.INP-12: It confirms that a probable cause determination under D.C. Code § 16-2312 is what supports continued protective custody.
relevance.DEC-04: It holds that a parent has no immediate appeal from the emergency removal and shelter care decision.
relevance.ACT-03: It defines the limited interlocutory review available once the child is placed in shelter care.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the jurisdictional bar that channels a parent's challenge to removal into the factfinding hearing rather than an immediate appeal.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: The warrantless entry into the apartment and seizure of an infant taken from a hospital nursery were justified by emergency circumstances, so the identification of the baby and the ensuing confession were not suppressed and the kidnapping conviction was affirmed.
cases.quote: Fourth Amendment law presumes that warrantless searches and seizures inside a home are unreasonable absent exigent circumstances

relevance.INP-03: It is the D.C. case on a police emergency entry to recover a missing child, the authority J.C. v. District of Columbia relies on for child seizures.
relevance.INP-12: It supplies the D.C. formulation of the exigency exception that governs taking a child from a home without a warrant.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the presumption against warrantless home entry that an emergency removal decision must overcome.
relevance.FAIL-02: It states the rule a plaintiff invokes when a child is taken from inside the home without a warrant or true exigency.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: Sitting en banc the court affirmed the dismissal of negligence suits against the District for failure to provide adequate police services, holding that the duty to furnish public services is owed to the public at large and that no individual can sue for its breach absent a special relationship giving rise to a specific legal duty to that person.
cases.quote: The duty to provide public services is owed to the public at large, and, absent a special relationship between the police and an individual, no specific legal duty exists.

relevance.OUT-06: It is the D.C. public duty doctrine that bars most negligence claims against the District arising from a child's injury or death unless the family can prove a special relationship.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the general rule of municipal non-liability out of which Turner v. District of Columbia carves the narrow child-abuse-reporting exception, so a brief citing Turner without it makes the District look far more suable than it is.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: The court affirmed the suspension of visitation, the change of permanency goal to adoption and the termination of parental rights, holding that the agency's case plan and reasonable efforts were adequate where the mother herself refused to participate in case planning and in the mental health services offered to her.
cases.quote: She cannot now argue, well after the fact, that the Agency should have done even more than it already did to overcome her uncooperativeness.

relevance.ACT-02: It holds that a parent who refuses to take part in case planning cannot later attack the court-ordered service plan as untailored or lacking benchmarks.
relevance.ACT-05: It affirms the suspension of a parent's visitation during a neglect case and holds that the magistrate judge was not required to rely on an explicit therapist recommendation to do so.
relevance.OUT-01: It is the necessary counterweight at the reunification node: a parent's own non-cooperation can supply the reasonable-efforts finding that permits the District to abandon reunification.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: The court affirmed retention of adoption as the children's sole permanency goal, holding that the case plan was appropriate and reasonable even though the mother never signed the plan documents and the later plan assigned no action components to the agency, and that the reasonable-efforts and inadequate-progress findings were supported by the record.
cases.quote: Thus, the case plan mirrored what the magistrate judge had ordered; it did not set out requirements that became effective only upon the Mother's signature.

relevance.ACT-02: It is the post-Ta.L. decision holding that a court-ordered case plan binds the parent without her signature because its requirements come from the court's own disposition order.
relevance.DEC-06: It measures a service response by whether the agency's case planning and efforts were reasonable and diligent, not by whether something more could have been done.
relevance.OUT-01: It is cited alongside In re K.C. for the proposition that a parent's refusal to cooperate bears on whether the government made the reasonable efforts required before reunification is abandoned.

cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
cases.holding: The court dismissed the mother's appeals for lack of jurisdiction, holding that an order changing a permanency planning goal is only a step toward final disposition, does not affect the parents' substantive rights, and therefore is not a final appealable order.
cases.quote: We hold accordingly that an order changing a permanency planning goal is not final or appealable.

relevance.FAIL-01: It is the rule In re Ta.L. overruled en banc in 2016, and candor requires citing it whenever Ta.L.'s appealability holding is relied on.
relevance.PMC-06: It governs the District's pre-2016 permanency record, in which goal changes from reunification to adoption were made with no possibility of appellate correction at all.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that ICWA § 1912(f)'s continued-custody standard does not apply where the Indian parent never had custody of the child and that § 1912(d)'s active-efforts requirement applies only where termination would precipitate the breakup of an existing Indian family, so neither provision barred termination of the biological father's rights.
cases.quote: Consistent with the statutory text, we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family's "breakup" would be precipitated by the termination of the parent's rights.

relevance.INP-11: It is the Supreme Court's construction of ICWA's active-efforts and continued-custody commands, which Holyfield (jurisdiction) and Brackeen (constitutionality) leave undefined, and it tells a District practitioner when those heightened duties actually attach.

cases.case_name: Monell v. New York City Dept. of Social Servs.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Municipalities and other local government units are 'persons' subject to suit under § 1983, but only where execution of the government's own policy or custom inflicts the constitutional injury; there is no vicarious liability for wrongs committed solely by employees.
cases.quote: We conclude, therefore, that a local government may not be sued under § 1983 for an injury inflicted solely by its employees or agents.

relevance.FAIL-02: It supplies the municipal-liability standard the District must be measured against on the remand ordered in Doe v. District of Columbia, which is the live theory once individual caseworkers obtain qualified immunity for a warrantless removal.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: A person involuntarily committed to a state institution retains substantive due process liberty interests in reasonably safe conditions, freedom from undue bodily restraint and minimally adequate training, and officials are liable only where their decision is a substantial departure from accepted professional judgment.
cases.quote: The State also has the unquestioned duty to provide reasonable safety for all residents and personnel within the institution.

relevance.ACT-03: It is the affirmative-duty case DeShaney relies on and the doctrinal basis for Smith v. District of Columbia: once the District takes a child into its custody and places him, it owes a constitutional duty of reasonable safety.
relevance.OUT-04: It explains why a youth who remains in a District placement past eighteen is still owed a constitutional duty of safe conditions and not merely statutory transitional services.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that an evidentiary hearing is not required before disability benefits are terminated and that what process is due is determined by weighing three factors: the private interest affected, the risk of erroneous deprivation under the existing procedures and the value of added safeguards, and the government's interest including administrative burden.
cases.quote: identification of the specific dictates of due process generally requires consideration of three distinct factors

relevance.DEC-05: It is the balancing framework In re S.J. applies in holding that denying a parent an immediate appeal from a shelter care order does not violate due process because the factfinding hearing follows.
relevance.DEC-03: It governs how much process a parent is constitutionally due before a substantiated finding and Child Protection Register listing take effect.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit
cases.holding: Sitting en banc the court held there is no 'jurisdictional question' exception to the law-of-the-case doctrine, so the later panel could not revisit the earlier panel's direction that the district court exercise pendent jurisdiction over the local-law claims in the foster care class action, and it remitted the District's remaining arguments to the panel.
cases.quote: the law-of-the-case and law-of-the-circuit doctrines precluded the panel in LaShawn II from revisiting the Gibbs step two decision reached in LaShawn I

relevance.INP-09: It is the appellate history that kept the LaShawn class action's systemic oversight intact, and it must travel on the face of any brief citing the 1991 merits findings.
relevance.FAIL-03: It preserved the local-law footing of the LaShawn remedial order, which is why the District's federal Title IV-E and IV-B shortfalls remained judicially enforceable in that case.
relevance.PMC-06: It fixes what the en banc court actually decided — law of the case and pendent jurisdiction, not the merits — so a cross-layer analysis does not overstate appellate endorsement of the District's systemic-failure findings.

notes: Court structure: the District of Columbia has no intermediate appellate court. The District of Columbia Court of Appeals (CourtListener court_id 'dc') is the jurisdiction's highest and only appellate court; D.C. Superior Court (including its Family Court magistrate judges) is the trial court and its opinions are generally not on CourtListener. Every 'dc' case in this brief is therefore a highest-court decision. The federal circuit for the District is the D.C. Circuit (cadc), with the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (dcd) below it.

All 40 cases were retrieved from the CourtListener v4 API in this session and their opinion text read. Every quote was programmatically verified to be an exact substring (whitespace and curly-quote normalized) of the opinion text, and each was checked to fall within the majority/lead opinion and before any concurrence or dissent in the same document.

EXCEPTION on the majority-opinion rule: the Troxel v. Granville quote is from Justice O'Connor's plurality opinion announcing the judgment (joined by three other Justices), not a five-Justice majority. It is the controlling opinion and is universally cited for the fit-parent presumption, but a lawyer should cite it as a plurality.

Two decisions have no reporter citation yet in CourtListener and are given in slip form: Geraci v. Hamilton, No. 22-CV-0749 (D.C. Feb. 5, 2026) and In re L.M., No. 23-FS-0386 (D.C. Dec. 21, 2023). Both are marked 'Published' by the court; Geraci carries the standard notice that it is subject to formal revision before publication in the Atlantic and Maryland Reporters, so the A.3d cite should be checked before filing.
No unpublished memorandum decisions were used. Every other entry is a published opinion with an official reporter citation.

ICWA (INP-11): there is no D.C. Court of Appeals or D.C. Circuit decision applying the Indian Child Welfare Act. A CourtListener search of court=dc for 'Indian Child Welfare Act' returned only In re Ta.L., which cites Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl for an unrelated proposition. INP-11 is therefore covered by the federal standard alone: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield (jurisdiction/domicile) and Haaland v. Brackeen (ICWA upheld). There is no D.C. authority on active efforts, qualified expert witnesses, placement preferences, or transfer to tribal court, and no District equivalent of a state ICWA.

Fourth Amendment caseworker searches and child interviews: a court=dc search for Fourth Amendment/caseworker/consent returned zero results. The only D.C. appellate treatment is J.C. v. District of Columbia, 199 A.3d 192 (D.C. 2018), which adopts the warrant/probable-cause/exigency framework and expressly declines to decide whether reasonable suspicion or probable cause is required for a warrantless child seizure under the exigency doctrine. Doe v. District of Columbia, 796 F.3d 96 (D.C. Cir. 2015), holds the point is not clearly established in this circuit, so individual caseworkers will normally have qualified immunity; municipal (Monell) liability is the live theory. There is no D.C. case on school interviews of children or on parental consent to investigative interviews.

Missing children from care (relevant to the PMC mission but not a listed node): no D.C. appellate decision addresses children who go missing from foster care. Oliver v. United States, 656 A.2d 1159 (D.C. 1995), the exigency case, involved an infant taken from a hospital nursery and recovered, and is the closest D.C. authority on the emergency-response side.

Oversight nodes (INP-09, PMC-01 through PMC-06): there is no D.C. case law on CFSRs, HHS OIG or Single Audit Act findings, CAPTA citizen review panels, or the Protect Our Kids Act commission. Those nodes are covered by the systemic-litigation record (LaShawn A. v. Dixon, 762 F. Supp. 959 (D.D.C. 1991), the merits trial decision in the 30-year LaShawn class action, affirmed in relevant part sub nom. LaShawn A. v. Barry, 87 F.3d 1389 (D.C. Cir. 1996) (en banc)) and by the D.C. FOIA cases. Lawyers should note that LaShawn A. v. Barry (en banc) resolved only law-of-the-case and pendent-jurisdiction questions, which is why it is not listed as a substantive authority here.

Damages practice warning for families: any tort claim against the District arising from a child's injury or death must satisfy the six-month written notice requirement of D.C. Code § 12-309, which Doe ex rel. Fein v. District of Columbia, 697 A.2d 23 (D.C. 1997), holds cannot be equitably tolled and is construed narrowly against claimants, even for an injured infant. District of Columbia v. Hampton, 666 A.2d 30 (D.C. 1995), then requires expert testimony on the social-work standard of care. Turner v. District of Columbia, 532 A.2d 662 (D.C. 1987), remains the gateway special-relationship holding.

Emergency removal procedure: D.C. Code § 16-2309 authorizes custody without a court order on reasonable grounds to believe the child is in immediate danger; § 16-2312 governs the shelter care hearing (probable cause, within 72 hours excluding Sundays); and § 16-2328(a) allows an interlocutory appeal only by the child, so a parent cannot immediately appeal a shelter care order (In re S.J., 632 A.2d 112 (D.C. 1993)). In re L.M. (2023) reached the merits because the child appealed.

Preservation/appeal trap: under In re Na.H., 65 A.3d 111 (D.C. 2013), a parent must move for review of a magistrate judge's order by a Superior Court associate judge within the time set by Super. Ct. Fam. R. D(e) or lose appellate review entirely. In re Ak.V., 747 A.2d 570 (D.C. 2000), preserves a late appeal only where excusable neglect is shown. Ineffective assistance of appointed counsel in a TPR must be raised on direct appeal by early motion (In re Petition of R.E.S., 978 A.2d 182 (D.C. 2009)).

The layers.case_law.key_cases already in the DC node files are keyword-matched noise and were discarded. 'In re Gumbinner', 'In re Larson-Jackson', 'In re Pisner', 'In re Wallace', 'In re Lee', 'In re Banks', 'In re Ross' and 'In re Hill' are D.C. Bar attorney-discipline opinions, not child-welfare cases. 'In re L.C.', 'Greene v. D.C. Child & Family Services Agency', 'In re Petition of K.D.W.' and 'In re Petition of S.U. & C.U.; C.J.' were not retrieved as on-point authority and are not carried forward. None of the pre-existing entries survived.

Doctrinal caution on In re Ta.L., 149 A.3d 1060 (D.C. 2016) (en banc): the opinion is fractured. Chief Judge Washington's opinion states the four holdings (due process at permanency hearings; preponderance finding of reasonable efforts before a goal change; appealability of the goal change; unfitness required before termination), but the separate opinions of Judge Glickman (concurring in the judgment) and Judges Beckwith and Easterly (concurring in part, dissenting in part) command different majorities on different parts. The quote used here is from the appealability holding, which overruled In re K.M.T., 795 A.2d 688 (D.C. 2002), and is uncontested as the judgment of the court. Counsel relying on the unfitness or weighty-consideration discussion should read all three opinions.

PMC-06 (Project Milk Carton AI analysis) has no case law of its own; it is mapped to the three authorities that define what the District's records and systemic findings actually are and whether they are publicly reachable.

Missing (for a later pass): Warren v. District of Columbia, 444 A.2d 1 (D.C. 1981) (en banc) — verified on CourtListener (cluster 2380714). This is the D.C. public duty doctrine case that Turner v. District of Columbia carves its special-relationship exception out of; Turner's own text cites it repeatedly and its footnote 11 says that but for the Child Abuse Prevention Act the court 'would, in all likelihood, be bound to affirm' under Warren. A brief that maps Turner to OUT-06 and FAIL-04 without Warren makes the District look far more suable than it is.

Missing (for a later pass): In re K.C., 200 A.3d 1216 (D.C. 2019) — verified on CourtListener (cluster 4586153). In re A.I. expressly relies on it (pincite 200 A.3d at 1238) for the proposition that the District's reasonable efforts are not negated by a parent's refusal to engage with services. It is the necessary counterweight at ACT-02 and OUT-01, where the brief currently presents reasonable efforts only from the parent-protective side.

Missing (for a later pass): In re J.M., 193 A.3d 773 (D.C. 2018) — verified on CourtListener (cluster 4536550). A post-Ta.L. reasonable-efforts and permanency-goal decision cited alongside K.C. in In re A.I.; belongs with In re A.I. at ACT-02, DEC-06 and OUT-01.

Missing (for a later pass): In re K.M.T., 795 A.2d 688 (D.C. 2002) — cite verified from the text of In re Ta.L. itself. This is the decision holding permanency goal changes non-appealable that Ta.L. overruled en banc. Any brief resting on Ta.L.'s appealability holding (FAIL-01, OUT-01, PMC-06) must cite the overruled case, both for candor and because pre-2016 records are governed by it.

Missing (for a later pass): Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl, 570 U.S. 637 (2013) — the Supreme Court's construction of 25 U.S.C. 1912(d) 'active efforts' and 1912(f) 'continued custody.' INP-11 currently rests on Holyfield (jurisdiction) and Brackeen (constitutionality) alone, neither of which tells a practitioner what active efforts require. In re Ta.L. itself cites Adoptive Couple, as the brief's own notes acknowledge.

Missing (for a later pass): Monell v. Department of Social Services, 436 U.S. 658 (1978) — the municipal-liability framework. Doe v. District of Columbia vacated summary judgment for the District and remanded precisely for Monell analysis, and the brief's own FAIL-02 blurb says municipal liability is 'the live theory,' yet the governing standard is nowhere in the case list.

Missing (for a later pass): Youngberg v. Romeo, 457 U.S. 307 (1982) — the state-custody affirmative-duty case DeShaney itself relies on (cited in the DeShaney text at the passage the brief quotes) and the doctrinal basis for Smith v. District of Columbia's holding that the District owed a substantive due process duty of care. Needed at ACT-03, OUT-06 and FAIL-04 to explain why custody changes the constitutional analysis.

Missing (for a later pass): Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976) — the balancing framework the brief invokes at DEC-05 through Lassiter, and which In re S.J. cites directly in rejecting the due process challenge to the parental interlocutory-appeal bar. It is doing real work in two nodes while being absent from the case list.

Missing (for a later pass): LaShawn A. v. Barry, 87 F.3d 1389 (D.C. Cir. 1996) (en banc) — the appellate history of the LaShawn class action, which the brief discusses in its notes but omits from the case list. A practitioner citing the 1991 district court merits findings for systemic propositions (INP-09, FAIL-03, PMC-01 through PMC-06) needs the subsequent history on the face of the brief, and the notes' caveat about what the en banc court actually decided should travel with the citation.

GAP-CLOSING PASS (2026-09-20). All nine authorities the verifier named were located on CourtListener, their clusters and opinions retrieved, and their opinion text read in this session; every one is real, published, and on point, and all nine were added. None failed verification, so there is no could-not-verify line below. Each added quote was programmatically confirmed to be an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text (whitespace, curly quotes and section-symbol spacing normalized) and to fall inside the majority/lead opinion, before any concurrence or dissent.

Added Warren v. District of Columbia, 444 A.2d 1 (D.C. 1981) (en banc) (cluster 2380714, opinion 2380714) for OUT-06 and FAIL-04: it is the en banc D.C. public duty doctrine holding that public services are owed to the public at large and that no individual may sue absent a special relationship. Candor note for readers: Warren is a police-response case, not a child welfare case, and the quote used is from Judge Nebeker's majority (the opinion also contains an appendix reproducing Judge Hannon's Superior Court memorandum and two partial dissents, neither of which was quoted). It is included because Turner v. District of Columbia is the exception to Warren's rule, and a brief that cites Turner alone overstates how suable the District is.

Added In re K.C., 200 A.3d 1216 (D.C. 2019) (cluster 4586153, opinion 4363406) for ACT-02, ACT-05 and OUT-01: it affirms the suspension of visitation, the goal change to adoption and TPR, and supplies the counterweight the brief lacked — a parent who refuses to engage in case planning and services cannot later fault the agency for not doing more. It also fills ACT-05 (protective orders/restrictions on contact), which previously rested on a single case, by holding that a magistrate judge need not have an explicit therapist recommendation before suspending visitation.

Added In re J.M. & D.M., 193 A.3d 773 (D.C. 2018) (cluster 4536550, opinion 4313803) for ACT-02, DEC-06 and OUT-01: the post-Ta.L. decision holding that a court-ordered case plan is reasonable and binding even though the parent never signed it and the later plan document assigned no action components to the agency, and that reasonable efforts are measured by whether the agency's planning and efforts were reasonable and diligent.

Added In re K.M.T., 795 A.2d 688 (D.C. 2002) (cluster 5138822, opinion 4958667) for FAIL-01 and PMC-06: the per curiam holding that a permanency-goal-change order is not final or appealable, overruled en banc by In re Ta.L. in 2016. It is listed for candor whenever Ta.L.'s appealability holding is relied on and because it governs how pre-2016 District goal-change records must be read. It is NOT mapped to OUT-01, which is already at the six-case ceiling with live authority.

Added Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl, 570 U.S. 637 (2013) (cluster 931616, opinion 931616) for INP-11: the Supreme Court's construction of ICWA § 1912(d) active efforts and § 1912(f) continued custody. This is a federal standard mapped because there is still no D.C. Court of Appeals or D.C. Circuit decision applying ICWA; INP-11 is covered by Holyfield, Brackeen and Adoptive Couple and by no District authority whatsoever.

Added Monell v. New York City Dept. of Social Servs., 436 U.S. 658 (1978) (cluster 109881, opinion 109881) for FAIL-02: the municipal-liability standard the District must be measured against on the remand ordered in Doe v. District of Columbia, 796 F.3d 96 (D.C. Cir. 2015). This is a federal standard mapped because no D.C. Court of Appeals decision states the policy-or-custom test; the District's own § 1983 exposure for removal policies is governed by Monell as applied in the D.C. Circuit.

Added Youngberg v. Romeo, 457 U.S. 307 (1982) (cluster 110746, lead opinion 9428825) for ACT-03 and OUT-04: the state-custody affirmative-duty case DeShaney relies on and the doctrinal basis for Smith v. District of Columbia. The quote is from Justice Powell's opinion of the Court, not from Justice Blackmun's concurrence. It was NOT mapped to OUT-06 or FAIL-04, both of which are already at the six-case ceiling; readers working those nodes should still read Youngberg through Smith and DeShaney.

Added Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976) (cluster 109382, opinion 109382) for DEC-05 and DEC-03: the three-factor due process balance that In re S.J., 632 A.2d 112 (D.C. 1993), applies in upholding the bar on a parent's interlocutory appeal from a shelter care order, and that governs how much process is due before a Child Protection Register listing takes effect. The quote is the clause naming the three-factor test; the three factors themselves (private interest; risk of erroneous deprivation and value of added safeguards; the government's interest including administrative burden) are set out in the holding field because quoting them in full would exceed the 30-word limit. This is a federal standard mapped because no D.C. decision independently formulates the test.

Added LaShawn A. v. Barry, 87 F.3d 1389 (D.C. Cir. 1996) (en banc) (cluster 721294, opinion 721294) for INP-09, FAIL-03 and PMC-06: the appellate history of the LaShawn class action. Readers must note what the en banc court actually decided — that there is no 'jurisdictional question' exception to law of the case, so the later panel could not revisit the earlier panel's pendent-jurisdiction direction — and not treat it as an affirmance of the 1991 merits findings on their substance. The case was remitted to the panel for the District's remaining arguments.

Node coverage after this pass: every one of the 42 nodes now carries between 2 and 6 cases. Three nodes were below two in the reconciled node_map — INP-04 (court-ordered referral), INP-09 (systemic audit/oversight trigger) and ACT-05 (protective order). No new authority was needed for INP-04 or ACT-05: In re K.I., 735 A.2d 448 (D.C. 1999) and In re Jam.J., 825 A.2d 902 (D.C. 2003) already carried those node ids in their own relevance maps and were simply missing from the node_map index, and In re K.C. was added to ACT-05. INP-09 gained LaShawn A. v. Barry alongside District of Columbia v. Hampton and Vining v. Council, which likewise already carried INP-09 in their relevance maps. The node_map has been reconciled throughout so that it now matches every case's relevance object; no existing case entry was altered.

Searches run for this pass (CourtListener v4, court=dc, cadc or scotus as appropriate): 'In re K.M.T. permanency goal' (dc), caseName searches for Monell, Youngberg/Romeo, Mathews/Eldridge and LaShawn (cadc), a citation search for '457 U.S. 307', and direct cluster retrievals for the three clusters the verifier had already identified (2380714, 4586153, 4536550). Full opinion text was retrieved and read for all nine additions before any entry was written.

Missing (for a later pass): Santosky v. Kramer, 455 U.S. 745 (1982) — the single most serious omission in the brief. Santosky is the constitutional floor holding that due process requires at least clear and convincing evidence before parental rights may be terminated. OUT-02 currently rests entirely on D.C. sources (In re Petition for Adoption of J.S.R., In re S.L.G., In re T.G.M.), and In re A.G. at OUT-03 distinguishes the clear-and-convincing standard for guardianship without the brief ever stating where that standard comes from. No competent termination brief omits Santosky.

Missing (for a later pass): Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County, 452 U.S. 18 (1981) — the case-by-case due process standard for appointed counsel in termination proceedings. The brief's own OUT-02 blurb for In re Petition of R.E.S. says the D.C. statutory right 'goes beyond Lassiter's case-by-case constitutional floor,' and its notes say Mathews is 'the balancing framework the brief invokes at DEC-05 through Lassiter' — the brief relies on Lassiter by name twice while never citing it.

Missing (for a later pass): Suter v. Artist M., 503 U.S. 347 (1992) — holds that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's 'reasonable efforts' requirement does not create a right enforceable by private plaintiffs under § 1983. This is the direct limit on FAIL-03 and on any attempt to read LaShawn A. v. Dixon as establishing privately enforceable federal rights; a brief that maps LaShawn and In re A.I. to 'federal compliance failure' without Suter materially overstates the remedy available.

Missing (for a later pass): Blessing v. Freestone, 520 U.S. 329 (1997) — the framework for when a federal spending-clause provision confers a § 1983-enforceable right. Needed alongside Suter at FAIL-03 to tell a practitioner whether Title IV-B/IV-E or CFSR shortfalls are actionable at all.

Missing (for a later pass): Smith v. Organization of Foster Families for Equality & Reform, 431 U.S. 816 (1977) — the Supreme Court's treatment of the liberty interest of foster families and the process due before a child is moved from a foster home. Nothing at ACT-03, ACT-04 or OUT-03 addresses the foster parent's or the child's own interest in placement stability, which is a routine issue in contested District permanency litigation. (Note also the name-collision risk with Smith v. District of Columbia, 413 F.3d 86, already in the brief.)

Missing (for a later pass): M.L.B. v. S.L.J., 519 U.S. 102 (1996) — an indigent parent may not be denied appellate review of a termination decree for inability to pay record preparation fees. It belongs at FAIL-01 beside In re Ak.V. and In re Na.H., which together present the District's appellate-preservation traps without the one constitutional rule that overrides a fee-based bar.

Missing (for a later pass): In re A.C., 573 A.2d 1235 (D.C. 1990) (en banc) — the leading D.C. en banc authority on court-ordered medical intervention and the substituted-judgment standard. In re K.I., which the brief maps at INP-04 and ACT-06, builds directly on In re A.C. and distinguishes it in choosing best interests over substituted judgment; citing K.I. without A.C. leaves the standard-selection holding unexplained.

Missing (for a later pass): In re S.J., 772 A.2d 247 (D.C. 2001) — holds that an order waiving a birth parent's consent to adoption is not final and appealable because it is only a step toward the final act of adoption. Verified from the text of In re K.M.T., which calls it 'dispositive.' It is the authority K.M.T. rests on and is therefore load-bearing for the brief's FAIL-01/PMC-06 appealability story, and it must be cited with care because the brief already maps a different In re S.J., 632 A.2d 112 (D.C. 1993), at four nodes.

Missing (for a later pass): Baker v. District of Columbia, 326 F.3d 1302 (D.C. Cir. 2003) — the D.C. Circuit's statement of the Monell policy-or-custom and deliberate-indifference standards as applied to the District specifically. FAIL-02 now maps Monell itself but nothing showing how this circuit applies it to the District, which is the actual question on the Doe v. District of Columbia remand.

Missing (for a later pass): Prince v. Massachusetts, 321 U.S. 158 (1944) — the foundational statement of the State's parens patriae authority and its limits. It is the necessary counterweight to Troxel at INP-05 and ACT-01, where the brief currently presents parental autonomy without the state-interest side of the balance.
